paper.subject: astronomy
paper.title: 12th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics — Observational Competition (Day)

documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
1. This part of the contest consists of 4 problems, is 1 hour long and is worth a total of 100 points.

2. Only blue pen should be used to fill in the answer boxes, draw and mark on the star chart.

3. You are not allowed to leave your working desk without permission. If you need any assistance (malfunctioning calculator, need to visit a restroom, etc.), please put up your hand to signal the supervisor.

4. The beginning and end of the competition will be indicated by a long sound signal.

5. Wait at your table until your envelope is collected. Once all envelopes are collected, your student guide will escort you out of the competition area.

documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
1. This part of the competition consists of 2 problems (O5 and O6), and is worth a total of 50 points.

2. You have 10 minutes to complete these problems.

3. Stop working once the timer expires.

4. At the end of the examination, hand over the test envelope to the supervisor at the station.

5. You will use a telescope to observe five red LED screens at a distance. The telescope is equipped with one eyepiece, but no finderscope. Some of these screens display the names of planets, some show Messier numbers, and some show equatorial coordinates.

transcription.notes: The PDF combines three separately paginated sheets: the Day observational competition (O1–O4, 4 problems, 1 hour, 100 points printed), the Night observational competition (O5–O6, 10 minutes, 50 points printed) and the Team Competition “Mountain” (no points printed). Therefore paper.totalPoints and paper.timeLimitMin are null; the printed totals and times are kept in paper.documentNotes (the two “Instructions” pages, p. 1 and p. 8). The year 2018 is not printed in the masthead; it is consistent with “March 21, 2018” in O3 and with the 12th IOAA. round is null because the catalogue value “observational” is not in the round vocabulary; roundType is observation although the Mountain task is a team practical (problemType practical). Parts: only O1 has printed sub-numbers (1)–(4), 20+5+10+5 = 40 points as printed. O4's Figures 4.1–4.4 each have an answer box but no printed sub-task labels, and O6 has five answer boxes without labels, so neither has parts; the catalogue's ~13 sub-tasks likely counted those boxes. The empty answer boxes and the “Answer：”/“Answers：” labels (printed with a full-width colon, and “Answer:” with an ASCII colon under Figure 4.4) are answer-sheet form elements and were not transcribed; the Mountain sheet's form lines “The height: ______ m; margin of error: ____ m.” and “Brief description of your process:” are kept in statementAfterParts, while “No. of Team:” and “Time of completion (for jury):” were omitted as jury form fields. Printed source quirks preserved: O1's first paragraph ends “in proportion to zenith distance” with no final period; the Mountain sheet prints “main concern ！” with a space and a full-width exclamation mark. The magnitude superscripts in O1 (5ᵐ, 1ᵐ - 3ᵐ, 2ᵐ) are written as LaTeX superscripts; the superscript “th” in “November 8th” is written inline as plain text. O5's first sentence is printed in bold, as is the whole O5 heading. The Mountain photo has no caption. No solutions file exists in the archive for this paper, so every solution is marked incomplete and no answers are given. No illegible passages.

problems.title: O1
problems.statement: Figure 1 is a whole sky star chart of Yanqing, Beijing at 20:30 tonight (UTC+8) with the limit magnitude = $5^{\mathrm{m}}$ (m = magnitude). Four stars (about $1^{\mathrm{m}}$ - $3^{\mathrm{m}}$) and one planet (brighter than $2^{\mathrm{m}}$) are missing in this chart. In the chart, the distance from the centre is in proportion to zenith distance

figures.caption: Figure 1
figures.alt: Circular whole-sky star chart: a large circle filled with black dots of different sizes (stars down to the limiting magnitude), with no coordinate grid, no constellation lines, no labels and no orientation marks.

parts.statement: Draw a cross (X) on the location of each missing star and mark “T” on the chart, and draw a cross (X) on the location of the missing planet and mark “P” on the chart.
Please mark the orientation of the star chart with “N” “E” “S” “W” at the edge of the star chart.
On the chart, the celestial equator passes through many constellations. Please write down the name of any five of these constellations (IAU codes).
Using the star chart, estimate the altitude of Aldebaran (α Tau), to the nearest degree.

problems.title: O2
problems.statement: Figure 2 is a star chart of a recent opposition of Jupiter. The grid in the figure is the ecliptic coordinates. Please estimate the date of this opposition, to the nearest day.

figures.caption: Figure 2
figures.alt: Star chart with an ecliptic coordinate grid: slightly tilted lines of ecliptic latitude 10°, 0° (thick line, the ecliptic) and −10°, and lines of ecliptic longitude labelled 300°, 290°, 280° and 270°. Dotted lines mark constellation boundaries. The label “Sgr” is at upper left; the stars of Sagittarius are joined by constellation lines and labelled with Greek letters (μ, λ, δ, γ, ε, σ, φ, τ, ζ, π, ο, ω, ρ, χ and others). A large black dot labelled “Jupiter” lies on the ecliptic just east of the 290° longitude line.

solution.incompleteReason: The archive has no official solutions file for this paper.

problems.title: O3
problems.statement: Figure 3 is a star chart of a part of the sky on March 21, 2018. The longitude and latitude of the observation site is 120°E, 40°N (UTC+8). The grid in the figure is an equatorial grid. The thicker vertical line in the centre is the meridian. Estimate the mean solar time to an accuracy of better than 0.5h.

figures.caption: Figure 3
figures.alt: Star chart of part of the sky with an equatorial grid: declination circles labelled 30°, 0° and −30°, and hour circles labelled 14h, 12h, 10h and 8h. A thick vertical line through the centre is the meridian, marked N at the top and S at the bottom. Stars are drawn as black dots joined by constellation lines, without constellation names. A grey band along the bottom of the chart shows the region below the horizon.

problems.title: O4
problems.statement: Figures 4.1 – 4.4 are four photos of Messier objects. For each of them, please write down the Messier catalogue number and name the constellation where it is located.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1
figures.alt: Black-and-white photograph of an irregular, roughly oval nebula made of bright tangled filaments over a diffuse glow, on a dark background with scattered stars.

figures.caption: Figure 4.2
figures.alt: Black-and-white photograph of an edge-on galaxy: a bright elongated central bulge crossed by a thin dark lane, on a dark background with scattered stars.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3
figures.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a roughly round nebula with two brighter lobes separated by a narrow waist, in a dense field of stars.

figures.caption: Figure 4.4
figures.alt: Tall black-and-white photograph of a large bright emission nebula with a dark intrusion at its upper left, a smaller separate nebulosity above it, and several bright stars below it, in a star field.

problems.title: Mountain
problems.statement:
**Instruction**

First and foremost, safety should be your main concern ！

You can see mountains around the hotel, and in the picture below, the highest peak is marked with an arrow. Estimate the height of this peak relative to the ground of the hotel. You can use everything you can get or make, except climbing up! The team which gives a number closest to the actual answer will win the ‘game’.

Give this page to the organizers or volunteers before 23:59, November 8th.
